extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students in philosophy of science, historians of science (especially chemistry), and researchers interested in evolutionary accounts of scientific practice
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual standards for judging when and how scientific practices behave as Darwinian populations and when their change amounts to epistemic, directional refinement. Focuses on copying fidelity, isolation, niche construction, stability of selective pressures, and community-level empirical practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-fidelity copying of scientific practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying of scientific practices must occur with high fidelity for directional refinement (selection-like processes) to operate on practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-fidelity copying enables reliable transmission of problem-solving strategies and methods across practitioners and generations, which in turn allows incremental improvement (directional refinement). Examples: Liebig’s lab and the Kaliapparat facilitated near-universal agreement on measurements because the practice was easy to copy. Anti-pattern: low-fidelity copying, where irregular transmission prevents cumulative refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease-of-use (facilitated copying) matters beyond formal standardization
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardization of methods is insufficient by itself; methods must be easy to learn and reproduce so that proficient use can be widely copied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A standardized method that is difficult to use will yield divergent results across users; by contrast, an easy-to-copy device or protocol (e.g., the Kaliapparat) both standardized practice and narrowed disagreement. Evaluation should consider practical learnability and reproducibility, not just formal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem complexity and labor-intensiveness that promotes decomposition and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems that are sufficiently complex or labor-intensive tend to be decomposed into smaller projects and distributed across multiple researchers, enabling wide copying of practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a problem exceeds what an individual can complete, it is split into manageable subprojects that can be reproduced across workers; this social organization fosters high-fidelity copying and accelerates community-level progress (as occurred after Liebig’s uptake of gap-filling, labor-intensive problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus/stabilization enabling practitioners to take assumptions for granted
rubrics_metrics.description: Widespread acceptance of certain facts, representations, or problem-solving approaches allows practitioners to take them for granted and pursue deeper or more refined inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following Kuhn, once a paradigm or near-universal practice is adopted, practitioners are relieved of re-justifying those items and can investigate more advanced questions. Measure includes the degree of community agreement and how that lowers justificatory burdens in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-level replication and inter-lab agreement as evidence against measurement error
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement among independent researchers and labs (using varied samples and conditions) weakens the measurement-error explanation and supports genuine phenomena, enabling shifts in research questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When different researchers routinely obtain similar results, it provides empirical grounds to question prior principles (e.g., 'one substance, one formula') and supports adopting new explanatory frameworks (e.g., structural chemistry). Evaluate the diversity of sources, replication practices, and whether inter-lab agreement was achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory-resources and personnel (capacity for massive testing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Development of certain research areas (e.g., structural chemistry) required intensive laboratory work and many practitioners; communities with greater lab infrastructure and available students advanced more rapidly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the community had sufficient lab space, instruments, and trained personnel to carry out the extensive empirical testing required by certain theories. Comparative example: Germany’s abundant labs vs. France’s relative paucity; Kekulé’s remark about dissertation topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Massive testing to adjudicate between competing structural models
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirming models that predict differing numbers of possibilities (e.g., isomers) requires extensive empirical search and testing until confidence that no further cases would have been found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directionality in such research depends on exhaustive experimental effort: test many combinations and sample conditions until the absence/presence of predicted entities becomes convincing. Anti-pattern: stopping too early and misattributing absence to theoretical failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic features (adaptedness) should explain differential reproductive success
rubrics_metrics.description: To treat practices as Darwinian-refractable, differences in practices' reproductive success should be explained substantially by their goodness-of-fit or adaptedness to selective pressures (intrinsicality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must evaluate how much of a practice’s spread is due to its intrinsic merits versus other contingencies. This aligns with the 'Intrinsicality Thesis' (in reference to Godfrey-Smith): assess whether intrinsic advantages, rather than drift or externalities, predict propagation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation from nonepistemic influences (epistemic niche construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A community’s ability to isolate its population of practices from nonepistemic (e.g., political, social, economic) influences increases the likelihood that selection on practices will be epistemic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the prevalence and efficacy of institutional filters, norms, and practices that prevent nonepistemic factors from determining which practices propagate. Communities that construct and maintain such epistemic niches are better candidates for directional epistemic improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective pressures should be epistemic (discriminating on knowledge-contribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The selection pressures acting on practices must discriminate between practices on the basis of how much they contribute to scientific knowledge, not on nonepistemic expediency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the nature of the pressures (publication incentives, funding, prestige, reproducibility standards) and whether they reward epistemic merit. If pressures mainly reward political or social expedience, directional change is not epistemic progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population size and susceptibility to drift
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller populations are poorer candidates for Darwinian populations because random drift and stochastic effects reduce the reliability of adaptedness differences in predicting reproductive success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider effective population size of practices: in small or fragmented research communities, chance and migration can dominate, undermining selection-driven refinement. Large, widely copying populations better realize selection on adaptedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Niche construction and ecological inheritance stabilize selective environment
rubrics_metrics.description: When a community (or organisms) constructs and transmits stable selective conditions across generations (ecological inheritance), directional refinement is facilitated because the phenotypic optimum remains stable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mechanisms by which communities stabilize selection-relevant conditions (tools, methods, institutions) so that selection can drive specialization. Examples: humans manufacturing environments; institutions that reproduce testing regimes and standards across time and space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability vs instability of selective pressures (favoring specialization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stable selective pressures reward specialization and allow mean trait values (or practices) to evolve toward an optimum; highly unstable pressures prevent directional refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess degree and temporal persistence of the pressures that matter for practice success. If pressures change frequently, incremental improvements are less likely to produce lasting increases in adaptedness. Use the stability continuum (total stability ↔ total instability) as analytic lens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation from introduction of deleterious/new variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection’s capacity to refine a population depends on how well the population is isolated from the continual introduction of new variants, which on average may be less well adapted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate migration, mutation, and other sources of variation (institutional cross-contamination, influx of non-adaptive practices) and whether community filters reduce their impact. Effective isolation increases selection’s efficacy in eliminating unfit variants and promoting epistemic refinement.
